Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

vignette: Martha, a 39-year-old European American woman and city council member, has spent years navigating life in the shadow of a traumatic event she witnessed during her childhood. Growing up, Martha was often present when her father would physically abuse her mother, an experience that continues to haunt her daily life. The clarity with which some moments of this violence come to mind contrasts sharply with the gaps where her memory fails her entirely. This partial recollection leaves her feeling both hyper-aware and disconnected from what actually transpired. In recent years, Martha has developed a deeply ingrained belief that she is only safe in very limited places, primarily within her home, which she now sees as a fortress of security. The trauma has made it almost impossible for her to feel comfortable anywhere else. This sense of safety is further reinforced by the fact that these memories are so vivid and intrusive; whenever they surface, Martha’s body seems to reenact the physical positions she was in during those moments, causing intense discomfort and fear. The clarity of some traumatic memories has heightened her hypervigilance. She spends a considerable amount of time observing people around her for signs that might indicate potential harm. This constant monitoring leaves her feeling perpetually on edge and makes it challenging to relax or fully engage with others. In particular, Martha's occupation as a city council member has become increasingly strained due to these symptoms. The public meetings she once enjoyed are now sources of anxiety; the crowded chambers trigger memories that make her feel physically vulnerable and mentally exhausted. Despite her best efforts to avoid these triggers, the intrusive nature of certain memories persists, often leading to sleep disturbances. Martha frequently wakes up in the middle of the night with vivid recollections of past events, which further erode her sense of security. This cycle of disrupted sleep and heightened threat perception has taken a toll on both her personal and professional life. Martha’s marriage is also affected by these symptoms. Her husband notices that she often retreats into herself during gatherings or social interactions, as the fear of encountering someone who might remind her of past violence becomes overwhelming. The tension in their relationship has increased due to her frequent avoidance behaviors and inability to fully engage with him and others outside their home. Recently, Martha felt compelled to seek help when a colleague at work expressed concern about her growing disengagement from city council duties. Her husband had also encouraged her to speak with someone, recognizing that she was struggling to maintain the balance between her public role and personal well-being. The most frightening aspect for Martha is not just the memories themselves but the persistent fear that they will never fully subside, leaving her perpetually on guard. Martha hopes that through therapy, she can find a way to reclaim some measure of safety outside her home and regain the ability to function without constant vigilance. Her underlying belief that such an outcome is possible provides a glimmer of hope amidst her fears.
